paragraphs: Testing a recommendation change is complicated when a platform connects consumers with producers. A producer’s experience depends on which consumers receive the change, so consumer treatment assignments also affect producer outcomes. The paper addresses how to design experiments that measure effects on the producer side of this connected marketplace.

The authors introduce a measure of experiment design quality and a mechanism called UniCoRn that constructs experiments using that measure. They prove that the design is optimal according to their proposed criterion. The approach also gives explicit control over experiment quality and computational cost, making those considerations part of the design process.

UniCoRn does not require advance knowledge of the producer-consumer network or assumptions about treatment propagation, and its approach is independent of network density. These properties matter for platforms whose connections change over time. The authors validate the method through simulations and report deployment in an edge recommendation application serving tens of millions of members. The optimality claim concerns their specific design quality measure.
neurips-2021-a-b-testing-for-recommender.tldr: UniCoRn designs producer-side recommendation experiments with explicit control over design quality and computation, without requiring a known consumer-producer network.

paragraphs: Deep kernel processes learn representations by repeatedly sampling kernel matrices and transforming them nonlinearly. The deep Wishart process is one such model. Its prior can match that of a deep Gaussian process when the kernels can be expressed entirely through Gram matrices, which describe relationships among representations.

The obstacle addressed here is inference: learning from observations requires a flexible approximation to the posterior distribution over positive semidefinite matrices. The authors construct such a distribution by generalizing the Bartlett decomposition of the Wishart density. They use it to build an approximate posterior that includes dependencies between layers, allowing uncertainty at different depths to be represented together.

The paper also develops a doubly stochastic inference procedure using inducing points. Experiments show that inference with the deep Wishart process can outperform inference with a deep Gaussian process having the equivalent prior. This result highlights the importance of the inference formulation: matching prior assumptions does not imply that different approximate inference methods will achieve the same empirical performance.
neurips-2021-a-variational-approximate-p.tldr: A flexible distribution over positive semidefinite matrices enables approximate inference in deep Wishart processes, with potential gains over equivalent-prior deep Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting a limited number of items to maximize a submodular objective when items arrive in random order. It considers both single-pass streaming and a secretary-style setting with shortlists. The central challenge is to obtain strong solution quality while retaining only a small amount of information about the stream.

For monotone objectives, the authors simplify an existing algorithm and its analysis while preserving a 1 − 1/e − ε approximation guarantee. Their improvement removes an exponential dependence on the accuracy parameter ε, bringing memory use to O(k/ε), where k is the selection limit. They also extend the techniques to non-monotone objectives, obtaining a 1/e − ε approximation with the same memory order.

The paper establishes a corresponding hardness barrier for the monotone random-stream setting, even with unlimited computation under the considered streaming constraints. Together, the algorithm and barrier clarify the attainable approximation quality in this model. Experiments on real datasets further support the practical usefulness of algorithms that the authors describe as simple to implement.
neurips-2021-cardinality-constrained-sub.tldr: Simpler random-stream algorithms achieve strong submodular maximization guarantees with O(k/ε) memory and exponentially improved dependence on the accuracy parameter.

paragraphs: Trajectory forecasting systems often model interactions among agents because one agent’s future movement depends on others. These interaction modules make predicted trajectories correlated. The paper argues that uncertainty associated with those correlations deserves explicit modeling, and introduces collaborative uncertainty to represent uncertainty arising from the interaction module.

The authors build a framework that learns future trajectories together with their uncertainty. It can be added as a plugin to existing forecasting systems. They develop versions based on multivariate Gaussian and Laplace distributions, providing two ways to represent the joint uncertainty rather than considering only separate trajectory predictions.

Experiments cover two synthetic datasets and two large forecasting benchmarks. On synthetic data, the framework reconstructs the underlying distribution well; on the forecasting benchmarks, it consistently improves the evaluated systems. One reported result is a 57-centimeter improvement in VectorNet’s final displacement error on nuScenes. Visualizations also associate collaborative uncertainty with the amount of interaction information among agents. These findings support treating interaction-related uncertainty as a useful component of joint forecasting.
neurips-2021-collaborative-uncertainty-i.tldr: Modeling uncertainty caused by interactions among agents improves the evaluated trajectory forecasters and helps represent their joint predictive distributions.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are appealing for online decisions because they represent uncertainty and support closed-form posterior updates. Their computational demands, however, grow substantially with the number of observations. Sparse variational Gaussian processes offer scalable inference for fixed datasets, but incorporating new observations efficiently remains difficult.

The paper introduces online variational conditioning, or OVC, to address that updating problem. OVC conditions a sparse variational Gaussian process on new data without requiring another round of training through the evidence lower bound. Its contribution concerns making an existing scalable model usable when information arrives incrementally and decisions must respond to it.

This capability allows sparse variational Gaussian processes to work with advanced look-ahead acquisition functions for black-box optimization, including settings with non-Gaussian likelihoods. Such functions consider possible future information when choosing what to evaluate next. The authors report compelling performance across applications including active learning of malaria incidence and reinforcement learning for simulated robotic control in MuJoCo. The findings support OVC as a practical connection between scalable uncertainty modeling and sequential decision-making.
neurips-2021-conditioning-sparse-variati.tldr: Online variational conditioning updates sparse variational Gaussian processes with new observations without retraining through the evidence lower bound.

paragraphs: A useful prediction interval should reflect how outcomes vary for a particular input, including whether their distribution is skewed. This paper develops a conformal prediction method for nonparametric regression that uses conditional histograms to adapt interval placement and width to the estimated shape of the outcome distribution.

A black-box learning algorithm first estimates that distribution using histograms. The proposed method converts those estimates into shortest prediction intervals targeting approximate conditional coverage. This connects a flexible distribution estimate to the practical question of how tightly an interval can contain the desired share of possible outcomes for an input.

The guarantees distinguish two kinds of reliability. Finite-sample marginal coverage is proved for the resulting intervals, meaning coverage averaged over inputs and outcomes. Conditional coverage and optimal interval length are achieved asymptotically if the underlying black-box model is consistent. Experiments on simulated and real data report improvements over conformalized quantile regression and other distributional conformal approaches. Thus, the stronger input-specific and length guarantees depend on the quality of the distribution estimator.
neurips-2021-conformal-prediction-using-.tldr: Conditional histograms yield adaptive conformal intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage and, under estimator consistency, asymptotically optimal conditional coverage and length.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a graph becomes difficult when only a tiny number have known labels. Although graph neural networks can use connections among nodes, their training can still deteriorate when direct supervision is extremely scarce. This paper develops Contrastive Graph Poisson Networks, or CGPN, specifically for that setting.

The framework combines a newly designed Graph Poisson Network with a conventional graph neural network, such as a Graph Attention Network. The Poisson component propagates the limited label information throughout the graph, while the conventional network guides that propagation flexibly. The construction is derived from variational inference, giving the combined learning approach a common foundation.

A contrastive objective extracts additional supervision from the learning processes of both components. The central idea is to make scarce labels useful across the graph through guided propagation and contrastive learning. Experiments across different dataset types report superior performance for CGPN. Those results support the proposed combination as a way to improve node classification when the amount of labeled data severely constrains ordinary graph neural network training.
neurips-2021-contrastive-graph-poisson-n.tldr: CGPN combines guided label propagation and contrastive learning to improve graph node classification when labeled examples are extremely scarce.

paragraphs: Offline learning asks an agent to improve using only a previously collected dataset. Reinforcement learning can potentially surpass the policies that generated the data, but bootstrapped value estimates can introduce extrapolation errors and unstable training. Direct imitation avoids that value-estimation mechanism, although imitating a mixture of policies can produce mediocre behavior.

Curriculum Offline Imitation Learning, or COIL, tries to retain the benefits of imitation while improving which behavior the agent follows. It builds on the observation that behavior cloning can imitate neighboring policies with less data. An experience-picking strategy selects behavior from adaptively chosen neighboring policies that have higher returns, creating a curriculum of successive improvements.

The curriculum makes the training target change with the current policy instead of treating all behavior in the dataset as equally desirable to copy. On continuous control benchmarks, COIL avoids merely learning mediocre behavior from mixed-policy datasets and is competitive with state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods. These results show that selective, staged imitation can be a strong approach to learning from fixed experience.
neurips-2021-curriculum-offline-imitatin.tldr: COIL improves offline imitation by progressively selecting higher-return neighboring behaviors, achieving competitive continuous-control performance without bootstrapped value learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot object detection must locate and identify new object categories from very few annotated examples. The paper treats generalization and category discrimination as related but distinct needs. It uses singular value decomposition to organize features into separate spaces for localization and classification.

Components associated with larger singular values form the generalization space used for locating objects. The motivation is that these components generally suppress some variations, such as style, while retaining intrinsic object characteristics. Components associated with relatively smaller singular values form the discrimination space because they may retain richer category-related information. Dictionary learning then extracts higher-level discriminative information from that space.

This division gives the two detection tasks feature representations chosen for their different purposes. Experiments on PASCAL VOC and COCO verify the method’s effectiveness, and visualization analysis supports its usefulness for few-shot detection. In the two-shot setting on VOC split1, the authors report a 6.2% improvement over their baseline. The explanation for using smaller singular components remains qualified: they may carry useful category information, rather than invariably doing so.
neurips-2021-generalized-and-discriminat.tldr: SVD-Dictionary enhancement separates features for localization and classification, improving few-shot object detection on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models help many language tasks, but adapting them can require more labeled examples than a target task provides. Grad2Task addresses few-shot text classification by learning from other tasks with rich annotations. The goal is to transfer useful adaptation behavior to tasks with only a small training set.

Its central choice is how to represent a task. Instead of using only encodings of the input texts, Grad2Task uses gradient information from a base model. Those gradients capture relationships between inputs and outputs, so the representation reflects what the task asks the classifier to learn. An adaptation network then modulates the classifier according to that task representation.

The approach is based on conditional neural processes and learns across diverse source tasks. Experiments on a collection of varied few-shot classification tasks show improvements over traditional fine-tuning, sequential transfer learning, and state-of-the-art meta-learning approaches. Additional analyses and ablations support the design choices. The findings suggest that information about how a task changes a model can be useful for deciding how to adapt that model.
neurips-2021-grad2task-improved-few-shot.tldr: Grad2Task represents tasks through model gradients and uses those representations to adapt text classifiers, improving performance on diverse few-shot tasks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how training with stochastic gradient descent gradually makes examples from different classes separable in a neural network’s feature space. The authors model feature evolution using one stochastic differential equation for each training sample. Each equation includes a drift term describing how backpropagation at one input affects the features of other samples.

The key property is local elasticity: an update has a stronger impact on samples from the same class as the input. Within the proposed equations, the authors identify a sharp transition. With local elasticity, features become linearly separable and training loss vanishes; without it, the features remain inseparable regardless of training duration.

The analysis also predicts neural collapse, a simple geometric organization of features, when local elasticity is present. Experiments on synthesized geometric shapes and CIFAR-10 corroborate the theoretical analysis. The significance is an explanation linking class-dependent update effects to the emergence of separable representations. The phase-transition statement belongs to the proposed dynamical model, rather than establishing an unrestricted condition for every neural network training procedure.
neurips-2021-imitating-deep-learning-dyn.tldr: A stochastic model of feature learning links stronger within-class update effects to a sharp transition toward linear separability and neural collapse.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether sparse linear regression can recover the interaction structure of an Ising model despite using a misspecified model. It analyzes typical learning behavior with the replica method from statistical mechanics. The main theoretical setting is typical random regular graphs in the paramagnetic phase.

Within that setting, the authors estimate the sample requirements of ℓ1-regularized linear regression and find it is consistent for model selection. Its sample complexity has the same logarithmic order in the number of variables as ℓ1-regularized logistic regression. This result concerns identifying interactions: a model’s mismatch to the data-generating mechanism does not necessarily prevent successful structure recovery in the analyzed regime.

The authors also provide an efficient way to predict finite-size behavior, including precision and recall for moderate sample counts and numbers of variables. Simulations agree fairly well with those predictions, even for graphs containing many loops. Although the analysis emphasizes linear regression, the method also applies to a broader class of ℓ1-regularized estimators, including logistic regression and interaction screening.
neurips-2021-ising-model-selection-using.tldr: For typical random regular Ising graphs in the paramagnetic phase, sparse linear regression can consistently recover structure with logarithmic-order sample complexity.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions provides groups of feature vectors and the fraction of positive labels in each group, rather than individual labels. This paper studies learning linear threshold functions from such groups, called bags. It shows that allowing bags containing just two examples can substantially increase computational difficulty.

When bags have size at most two and are consistent with an unknown linear threshold function, the authors give an efficient algorithm satisfying at least two-fifths of them. If every bag contains two differently labeled examples, the guarantee improves to one-half. For targets that are OR functions on d-dimensional Boolean inputs, they obtain an additional improvement of order 1/d.

The hardness result shows that, even when a monotone OR satisfies every non-monochromatic bag, obtaining a constant improvement beyond one-half is NP-hard using any function of constantly many linear threshold functions. This contrasts with ordinary supervised learning, where consistent linear thresholds can be learned efficiently to arbitrary accuracy. The distinction arises from losing individual labels, even in very small bags.
neurips-2021-learnability-of-linear-thre.tldr: Replacing individual labels with proportions for pairs of examples creates sharp computational barriers to learning linear threshold functions.

paragraphs: Neural networks that fit the same training data can differ substantially in how well they generalize. This paper focuses on the complexity of the particular function learned, motivated by evidence that lower Kolmogorov complexity is associated with better generalization among functions that fit training data well.

The authors introduce Kolmogorov Growth, a complexity measure used to derive generalization error bounds depending on the final classification function. Guided by those bounds, they develop network-to-network regularization, which constrains the training trajectory to remain in a region of low Kolmogorov Growth. The approach turns a preference for simpler functions into a constraint applied during learning.

Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 across different training-set sizes report clear generalization improvements. Conventional training produces higher Kolmogorov Growth and lower test accuracy in their empirical studies. With corrupted training labels, the method achieves competitive performance and significantly improves over standard cross-entropy baselines in most cases. These results support the proposed complexity preference without establishing that it explains every aspect of neural network generalization.
neurips-2021-network-to-network-regulari.tldr: Network-to-network regularization constrains Kolmogorov Growth during training and improves generalization in the evaluated image-classification settings, including noisy labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies how complex a neural representation must be to approximate solutions of high-dimensional elliptic partial differential equations. It works with Barron spaces, whose functions admit integral representations built from parameterized ridge functions. This setting connects properties of the equation’s ingredients to the representational complexity of its solution.

Under appropriate assumptions, the authors prove that when the equation’s coefficients and source term belong to Barron spaces, its solution can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a Barron function in the H1 norm. They also bound the Barron norm of that approximating function, making the dependence on the equation’s dimension explicit and at most polynomial.

These estimates imply that a two-layer neural network can approximate the solution on any bounded domain with an explicit dimension-dependent convergence rate in H1. The contribution provides a conditional theoretical foundation for neural approximation of these equations. It establishes representational possibility and complexity bounds under the stated structural assumptions, rather than making a claim about all high-dimensional PDEs.
neurips-2021-on-the-representation-of-so.tldr: Under suitable Barron-space assumptions, elliptic PDE solutions admit controlled Barron approximations and two-layer neural approximations with explicit dimension-dependent rates.

paragraphs: ParK is a solver designed to make kernel ridge regression practical on large datasets. The paper’s central concern is reducing memory and computation while retaining statistical accuracy. Its approach combines partitioning, random projections, and iterative optimization, so efficiency comes from several coordinated parts of the solver.

The distinctive choice is to construct suitable partitions in feature space rather than directly in input space. These partitions encourage orthogonality among local estimators, reducing their overlap in the representation used by the model. The analysis uses this structure to keep important statistical quantities, including local effective dimension and bias, under control.

The authors prove that their approach can reduce space and time complexity while maintaining the same statistical accuracy, and characterize the resulting tradeoff between statistical and computational demands. Numerical experiments on large datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The broader contribution is a principled explanation of how dividing a kernel problem can preserve accuracy: the geometry of the partition matters alongside the computational savings from solving smaller local problems.
neurips-2021-park-sound-and-efficient-ke.tldr: ParK uses feature-space partitions, random projections, and iterative optimization to reduce kernel ridge regression costs while provably preserving statistical accuracy.

paragraphs: Forecasting collections of many time series creates an opportunity to learn across related sequences. A useful forecast should also describe possible outcomes rather than supply only a single predicted value. The paper introduces Level Set Forecaster, or LSF, as a general method for turning a point estimator into a probabilistic forecaster.

The authors connect their construction to random forests and quantile regression forests. Those connections allow them to prove consistency guarantees under mild assumptions on the underlying point estimator. The theoretical result therefore depends on properties of the model being converted; it does not assert that every arbitrary point predictor automatically yields a consistent probabilistic forecast.

The analysis also produces consistency results for quantile regression forests using the CART splitting criterion, which the authors identify as the first such results. In experiments, LSF equipped with tree-based point estimators rivals state-of-the-art deep learning models in forecasting accuracy. The findings show that a relatively simple conversion approach can offer competitive forecasting performance while supporting a theoretical analysis of its probabilistic estimates.
neurips-2021-probabilistic-forecasting-a.tldr: Level Set Forecaster converts point predictors into probabilistic forecasters, with conditional consistency guarantees and competitive results using tree-based models.

paragraphs: Research on fairness in tabular machine learning has relied heavily on the UCI Adult dataset. The authors reconstruct a superset of that dataset from available US Census sources and identify peculiarities that limit how broadly conclusions drawn from it can apply. This motivates expanding the evidence used to evaluate fairness methods.

The paper’s main contribution is a suite of Census-derived datasets with prediction tasks covering income, employment, health, transportation, and housing. The data include multiple years and every US state. That coverage lets researchers examine whether findings persist across time and geography, rather than treating one dataset as representative of many deployment settings.

An initial empirical investigation explores tradeoffs among fairness criteria, the performance of algorithmic interventions, and distribution shift. The authors report findings that challenge some existing narratives and suggest new research directions. The value of the contribution is both practical and methodological: it supplies additional benchmarks and makes variation across populations and time an explicit part of evaluating claims about fair machine learning.
neurips-2021-retiring-adult-new-datasets.tldr: New Census-derived datasets broaden fairness research beyond UCI Adult and enable studies of geographic variation, temporal shift, and intervention performance.

paragraphs: Estimating human poses in crowds is difficult because people overlap and hide parts of one another. These conditions make both person bounding boxes and individual body keypoints unreliable. The paper introduces PINet, a network that infers complete pose cues directly from visible body parts without requiring bounding-box detection or keypoint grouping.

PINet first generates several coarse pose estimates for each person from their body parts. A refinement module improves these estimates using pose priors, and a fusion module combines them. The method uses distinctive visible parts to distinguish overlapping people while drawing on body appearance cues to infer a person’s overall pose.

This design connects partial visual evidence directly to whole-person hypotheses, addressing the difficulty of assembling poses from separately detected keypoints in crowded images. Experiments on several crowded-scene benchmarks demonstrate the method’s superiority in the reported comparisons. On OCHuman, PINet achieves 59.8% average precision and outperforms recent work by a large margin. The results support direct pose-level inference as an effective strategy for the evaluated overlap and occlusion settings.
neurips-2021-robust-pose-estimation-in-c.tldr: PINet estimates whole-person poses from visible body parts, improving crowded-scene pose estimation without bounding-box detection or keypoint grouping.

paragraphs: Systems such as traffic scenes can be represented as geometric graphs, with objects as nodes positioned in space. Their coordinates depend on an arbitrarily chosen global reference frame. For the systems considered here, rotating or translating that frame does not change the governing dynamics, so a learned interaction model should respect those invariances.

The paper introduces a local coordinate system for each object. These local frames build rotation and translation invariance into the geometric graph representation. They also provide a natural basis for anisotropic graph filtering, meaning that a graph neural network can treat interactions differently depending on their direction in an object’s local frame.

This combination lets the model represent directional interactions while respecting the arbitrariness of global coordinates. The authors motivate the approach through the poorer generalization that can result from ignoring these invariances. Experiments on traffic scenes, three-dimensional motion capture, and colliding particles show the method comfortably outperforming recent state-of-the-art approaches. The findings support local reference frames as a useful structural choice for learning the evaluated interacting dynamical systems.
neurips-2021-roto-translated-local-coord.tldr: Object-specific coordinate frames encode rotation and translation invariance while supporting directional graph interactions, improving predictions across three dynamical-system settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a graphical model that evolves over time. Its structural assumptions are that the graph is sparse and that only a sparse set of relationships changes between time periods. These assumptions create an opportunity to estimate a changing system while avoiding the cost of treating every period as an unrelated problem.

The authors introduce constrained optimization problems based on exact ℓ0 regularization, which directly represents sparsity. Their formulation can be solved using near-linear time and memory. They also prove a small estimation error and develop statistical guarantees for high-dimensional settings, addressing both computational efficiency and the reliability of the inferred model.

Under the studied conditions, the analysis shows that learning can be possible with as little as one sample per time period. This is a result for sparsely changing Gaussian Markov random fields, not an unrestricted promise for arbitrary evolving graphs. In practice, the authors report accurate estimation of models with more than 500 million variables in under an hour, demonstrating the approach’s substantial computational scale.
neurips-2021-scalable-inference-of-spars.tldr: An exact-sparsity formulation enables near-linear inference for sparsely changing Gaussian graphical models, with strong estimation guarantees and large-scale empirical results.

paragraphs: Derivative observations can improve Gaussian process regression by supplying information about how a function changes. Incorporating them directly is expensive: the stated training cost grows as O(N³D³), with N observations and D input dimensions. The paper targets settings where both the dataset and dimensionality are large.

The authors introduce inducing directional derivatives to compress derivative information, analogous to using inducing values to summarize function observations. This construction supports a variational posterior whose size depends on neither the full number of data points nor the full input dimensionality. It provides a compact uncertainty representation while still incorporating information about the function’s derivatives.

Experiments demonstrate scalability across tasks including high-dimensional stellarator fusion regression and Bayesian optimization for training graph convolutional networks on PubMed. The authors also find that the approach can improve regression when only labels are available. That empirical observation extends its potential usefulness beyond datasets with observed derivatives. The main computational contribution is the compressed posterior construction; independence of its size from N and D should not be read as every computation being independent of them.
neurips-2021-scaling-gaussian-processes-.tldr: Inducing directional derivatives enable compact variational Gaussian process regression with derivative information in large, high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Standard recurrent neural networks process sequences through a chain of repeated operations. The paper proposes a different architectural bias: a recurrent unit that can recursively instantiate itself, with the extent of recursion changing across a sequence. This is intended to provide flexibility for varied data expressed in sequential form.

In the self-instantiated recurrent unit, or Self-IRU, instances of the unit itself control its gating mechanisms through recursive invocation. Gates with values between zero and one regulate the extent of recursion. Because those gate values can vary over time, the architecture supports a soft, dynamically changing recursion depth at each sequence position.

The authors demonstrate the architecture’s effectiveness across multiple data modalities. On a logical inference dataset, Self-IRU achieves state-of-the-art performance even against competitive models supplied with ground-truth syntactic information. That comparison supports the usefulness of the recursive architectural bias for the evaluated task. More broadly, the contribution is a recurrent building block that explicitly represents dynamic recursion as part of its design, alongside evidence that this flexibility can benefit sequence learning.
neurips-2021-self-instantiated-recurrent.tldr: Self-IRU adds gated, dynamically varying soft recursion to recurrent networks and demonstrates strong performance across multiple data modalities.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks and deep ensembles can quantify predictive uncertainty, but storing their parameters often requires substantially more memory than a deterministic network. This paper addresses that storage burden by representing uncertainty in a lower-dimensional space associated with each network weight matrix.

The method augments each weight matrix with a small inducing weight matrix. These inducing weights provide the compact space in which uncertainty is represented. The authors also extend Matheron’s conditional Gaussian sampling rule to sample network weights quickly. That sampling component matters because reducing storage alone would not make the approach practical if drawing weights remained too expensive.

Experiments with fully connected networks and ResNets show competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods on prediction and uncertainty estimation tasks. The authors report reducing parameter size to at most 24.3% of that of a single neural network while maintaining reasonable runtime relative to ensembles. The findings support a compact uncertainty representation as a way to reduce memory demands without giving up competitive predictive and uncertainty-estimation performance in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-sparse-uncertainty-represen.tldr: Small inducing weight matrices compress neural-network uncertainty, enabling fast sampling and competitive prediction with sharply reduced parameter storage.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes normalized neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, momentum, and weight decay. Earlier discussions often examined an equilibrium where the weight norm stays constant. The authors instead investigate why that equilibrium can arise, treating it as a particular state within what they call Spherical Motion Dynamics.

They introduce assumptions that lead to equilibrium and prove a linear-rate convergence regime under those assumptions. They also propose angular update as an alternative to effective learning rate for describing the dynamics. This quantity focuses on how weight direction changes, and the authors derive its theoretical value at equilibrium.

Experiments on large-scale vision tasks, including ImageNet and MSCOCO with standard settings, test the assumptions and theoretical predictions. The reported observations agree well with the theory. The paper also shows that angular-update behavior can affect practical network optimization. Its contribution is a conditional account of how equilibrium develops and a different quantity for tracking training motion, rather than simply assuming that a stable weight norm has already been reached.
neurips-2021-spherical-motion-dynamics-l.tldr: Spherical Motion Dynamics explains equilibrium in normalized-network training under stated assumptions and uses angular updates to characterize that behavior.
